4e487f0922: Genoryn Krypton (GNR) Documentation: Wallet, Mining, Swaps, API
be0c07c7b6: Everything you need to use, mine, trade, run, integrate and audit Genoryn Krypton: quantum-resistant, private-by-default money with a fair launch, a 21,000,000 GNR cap and atomic swaps with bitcoin. Start with the quick start, or jump to any topic from the contents.
dd252001fe: Genoryn Krypton (ticker <0>GNR</0>) is a proof-of-work cryptocurrency built so that <1>no elliptic curve protects your coins or your privacy</1>. Spends are authorized by zk-STARK proofs over hash functions, every transfer is shielded, notes are encrypted with NIST's post-quantum ML-KEM, and light wallets verify the chain themselves without downloading it. GNR and bitcoin are traded peer to peer with atomic swaps: no exchange, no custody, no account.
e91e65590f: Every transfer shielded (zk-STARK); no transparent mode
0ff30c863e: Shared by every miner in proportion to its work, no pool needed
84dc11bfa8: Atomic BTC ⇄ GNR swaps on an anonymous offer board; the seller's GNR is locked first
b8a5e7c5a9: FlyClient-style tip proofs, follow the most work, release checkpoint (block 14,800)
d15f02faaa: <0>What makes it different</0>, in one paragraph each:
754052f709: <0>Quantum-resistant end to end.</0> Coin ownership is proven with hash-based STARKs, encryption is hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM, releases are signed with ML-DSA and SLH-DSA. A quantum computer that breaks elliptic curves breaks nothing here.
79497c63ae: <0>Private by default.</0> Amounts, senders, recipients and memos are hidden for everyone, always. There is no "transparent" address type that would shrink the anonymity set.
ea49f5d26a: <0>Fair mining.</0> Every block's reward is split among all miners by their share of the work, so a single GPU earns its exact share every block without joining a pool, and no operator stands between miners and their coins.
9df6496184: <0>Trustless trading.</0> The wallet swaps GNR and bitcoin with another wallet directly. Nobody can sell GNR they do not have: the seller's coins are locked on chain before the buyer pays.
082355520b: <0>Install.</0> Download the Windows installer or the Linux package from <1>Download</1> (see <2>Install & verify</2>), or build from source.
5184eaff4c: <0>Create a wallet.</0> Open the wallet, choose a password and write down the recovery phrase: 24 words, each with a two-digit number, on paper. Nobody, including the project, can restore a wallet without it.
6deb948871: <0>Get coins.</0> Mine from the <1>Mining</1> tab, buy with bitcoin in the <2>Swap</2> tab, or share your short address (<3/>) to receive.
6a31bee330: <0>Send privately.</0> Enter an address and an amount; a zero-knowledge proof is built on your computer in about half a second and only then sent.

Press <1>Publish short form</1> once: it goes to genoryn.io, your configured nodes and your own node, and the wallet shows where it resolves. Share the short form (<2/>); a sender's node resolves it and the sender's wallet checks that the answer hashes to it, so a node cannot substitute another recipient. A QR code is shown for both forms.

031dc19fbd: A transaction spends at most two notes. When a payment needs more, the wallet merges notes automatically in parallel rounds (one block per round) and then pays.
f3669b6d15: Paged (15 to 100 entries per page) with filters for received, sent, mining and pending, search by memo, txid, address or block, and totals. Each send has a <0>Proof</0> button for a <1>payment proof</1>. <2>View ↗</2> opens a payment's transaction on the genoryn.io explorer, <3>Block ↗</3> the block that holds it, and the block number is a link too. The explorer shows that the transaction exists, its block and its fee, never the amount or the parties.

Taking an offer starts a swap at once; when it is time to pay, a window shows the amount, the address and a QR code. An offer can <1>follow the market price</1> by itself, within a limit you set. See <2>Atomic swaps</2>.
1f0faea012: Choose <0>Automatic</0>, <1>NVIDIA</1> (CUDA), <2>AMD / Intel</2> (OpenCL) or <3>CPU</3> with a CPU-usage cap, then <4>Start mining</4>. The tab shows your hashrate, your share of the network, expected GNR per day, shares found, accruing rewards, payouts and the <5>mining and price calculator</5>. If the miner stops, the tab shows why (for example a GPU driver error); it is restarted automatically, and after three quick failures in a row the wallet stops retrying and says so. While the miner runs, closing the window keeps the wallet, node and miner running; <6>Quit</6> stops everything.
ba567e17cd: Charts of hashrate, supply, active miners, difficulty, issuance, block time, shares and transactions per block over 1 hour to all time; block finders; peers; and the <0>connection mode</0>:
06869f8a67: <0>Light</0> (recommended): remote nodes provide data; headers, outputs and tree updates are verified on your computer (<1>Light clients</1>). Several nodes can be configured; they are cross-checked.
7a665e7ce3: <0>Full node</0>: one click starts <1/>, which downloads and validates the whole chain; the wallet then uses only your own node. By default it connects only out to other nodes; <2>Let other nodes connect to my full node</2> accepts incoming peers too (<3>Peer-to-peer network</3>).
214f967038: <0>Proxy (Tor)</0>, optional: the wallet's own connections (the nodes it reads, the offer board, the Bitcoin service, the BTC price and updates) go through a SOCKS5 proxy, so those servers see the proxy's address instead of yours. Use <1/> for Tor or <2/> for Tor Browser; only <3/> is accepted, so names are resolved through the proxy too. It applies from the next start of the wallet, changing it needs the wallet password, and a node or Bitcoin Core on this computer is still reached directly.
c9bd0028e3: A line to type commands on, as Bitcoin's wallet has, with their answers above it. It completes commands as you type (<0>Tab</0>), brings back earlier lines with the arrow keys, and <1/> lists everything. Commands about the chain (<2/>, <3/>, <4/>, <5/>, <6/> and more) go to the node the wallet uses; commands about the wallet (<7/>, <8/>, <9/>) are answered on your computer. <10>The console only reads</10>: no command can send GNR, show a recovery phrase or a key, or change a setting, so nothing pasted into it can take your coins. See <11>User interface</11>.
bf1d0ef975: Change a wallet's password and lock wallets; see the version, check for updates and choose whether updates install automatically.
8f41a56a1a: The <0>recovery phrase</0> is the wallet. It consists of 24 tokens of the form <1/>: an English BIP-39 word and a number from 00 to 63, 17 bits each. Together they carry 384 bits of entropy and a 24-bit SHA3 checksum, so a mistyped token is detected. Everything else (keys, addresses, notes, mining rewards) is derived from or found again with it.
d2baa496ac: <0>Write it on paper</0> (or metal), in order, with the numbers. Never type it into a website, a chat, an email or a photo. Anyone who has it owns the coins.
198f370c5f: <0>Restore</0>: Wallet → <1>Add a wallet</1> → restore, or <2/>, then let it sync. A phrase of 24 words without numbers (BIP-39, as Genoryn Mainnet 1.0 and other wallets made them) restores too: type its words as they are. Positions written next to the words (<3/>, <4/> …) and commas may stay. Mainnet 1.0 was a separate, earlier chain: its coins are not on Genoryn Krypton.
4632845536: <0>The wallet file</0> (<1/> or <2/>) is encrypted with Argon2id (256 MiB of memory) and XChaCha20-Poly1305 under your password. Copying it is a convenient backup of your history and swap records, but only the phrase guarantees access.
570eba4e9e: <0>Swaps in progress live in the wallet file.</0> If you restore from the phrase while a swap is running, finish or refund it from the old file if you still can. From 1.0.33 a restored wallet never reuses an earlier swap's secret, keys or outputs.
9ae78898aa: <0>Lost the password but have the phrase?</0> Restore from the phrase and choose a new password. <1>Lost the phrase but have the file and password?</1> Show the phrase (Security tab, or <2/>) and write it down now.
8ad2d017a9: <0>Password for anything that moves coins.</0> Sending, publishing or taking an offer and starting or accepting a swap ask for the wallet's password every time. The session token alone, which other programs of your user could read, cannot spend. After five wrong passwords the wallet refuses for five minutes.
e98bb3103f: <0>Auto-lock.</0> An unlocked wallet stays open for 24 hours, then locks itself and asks for its password again. The miner keeps running; swaps wait for the wallet to be unlocked (their timelocks leave hours of room).
609012c59d: <0>Local only.</0> The wallet's server listens on <1/>, checks a random token on every request and refuses requests addressed to any other host name, so a web page you visit cannot talk to it (DNS rebinding).
eed3b1ed7c: <0>Nothing reaches your computer from the internet.</0> The wallet's own full node only connects out unless you allow incoming peers, its API listens only on this computer, and it never runs commands or reads files for other nodes.
1efcba38e5: <0>Signed updates only.</0> The updater installs a release only if its post-quantum signature verifies against the key compiled into the wallet (<1>Updates</1>).
e0848f8248: <0>Your computer is your responsibility.</0> Malware running as your user can read your screen and keystrokes; keep the system updated, the phrase offline, and use a strong, unique password.
da369c7ee5: The wallet checks GitHub for a newer release. It downloads <0/>, verifies its hybrid ML-DSA-87 + SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256s signature against the release key compiled into the program, downloads the installer and checks it against the signed hash. Only then does it install. A compromised download host, CDN or GitHub account cannot push code without the release key.
b37091b91a: <0>About → Check for updates</0>, or the offer that appears when a release is out. <1>Install updates automatically</1> installs them as soon as they are found.
33ef6e9616: Your wallets, settings and chain data carry over; a running miner resumes by itself after the update.
6b22fc9545: Release notes list what changed and whether consensus changed. Security fixes are announced in general terms first and in detail once most wallets have updated.
9e816754f8: Coins live as <0>notes</0>: <1/> hidden inside a commitment <2/> in a Merkle tree of depth 40. Spending a note reveals only its <3>nullifier</3>, a hash of a secret key and the note position, which prevents double spending without revealing which note was spent.

a25a01f74d: Mining income is public per miner (as coinbase rewards are on every chain); mine to a separate wallet if you want it unlinked from your receiving address. Spending mined coins is as private as any other spend. There is no transparent mode, so every user shares the same anonymity set.
99b2cd3a0a: <0>On the network:</0> peer connections are encrypted end to end; your own transactions are first relayed to a single random peer and announced to everyone only after 20 seconds, which hides their origin. The public node's API never lists peers' IP addresses.
989aca4bce: <0>Your IP address</0> is not on chain, but the servers a light wallet talks to see it. Set a Tor proxy in Network → Connection mode to hide it from them. The full node (<1/>) has no proxy setting: its peers see its address. If that matters, use the light wallet over Tor, or run the node with <2/> so nothing can connect to it.
a252d2c9ca: <0>On the offer board:</0> every offer has its own one-time post-quantum key, never your address, so offers cannot be linked to you or to each other. Messages between the two wallets of a swap are sealed so that the board cannot read them. A swap's bitcoin side is an ordinary Bitcoin transaction and is as public as any other.
45793baccd: Keys derive deterministically from the recovery phrase. SHAKE256 turns its 384 bits into a spend secret, a hybrid KEM key pair and an ML-DSA key. The spend secret yields an authorization key <0/>, a nullifier key <1/> and an owner tag <2/>; view-only wallets can hold <3/> without being able to spend. A separate swap seed derives the one-time board keys and the per-swap secrets and keys.
0547b62545: <0>Shor's algorithm</0> breaks RSA and elliptic curves (ECDSA, Ed25519, Pallas, BLS). None of them protect Genoryn Krypton coins: spends are proofs of knowledge of a hash preimage, verified with hash-based STARKs. Encryption is hybrid, so recorded traffic stays secret as long as <1>either</1> X25519 or ML-KEM holds ("harvest now, decrypt later" is defeated by ML-KEM).
83a202792b: <0>Grover's algorithm</0> square-roots brute force: 256-bit hashes and keys keep a 128-bit margin; the 384-bit recovery phrase keeps 192 bits; STARK soundness parameters target about 160 conjectured bits.
447f6ce80c: <0>The bitcoin side of a swap</0> uses Bitcoin's own secp256k1 keys, as every Bitcoin transaction does. They protect the bitcoin only for the few hours a swap runs.
3fc45e9ee0: Every primitive has a versioned identifier, so a weakened algorithm can be replaced by a soft fork without stopping the network.
586cd013f3: The schedule follows Bitcoin's shape on 60-second blocks. Block <0/> issues <1/> into the reward pool; the genesis issues nothing. Fees join the pool too, and the pool pays miners in proportion to their shares (<2>Mining rewards</2>). That is 7,200 GNR a day in the first era.
6209cacf11: After 29 halvings the reward reaches zero; total issuance stays below 21,000,000 GNR by less than one coin of integer rounding. Every node rejects a block that would exceed the cap. Live figures: <0/> and the explorer.
8683db5232: A common way to express how rare a coin is, is <0>stock-to-flow</0>: the coins that exist divided by the coins mined in the following year, i.e. how many years of mining are already stored. Gold is about 60. Every halving doubles it. The figures below follow from the schedule alone.
d78176a62f: GNR reaches gold's scarcity around 2041 and that of Bitcoin in 2026 (about 122) around 2045. Bitcoin, which started 17 years earlier, keeps getting scarcer too. Scarcity is a property of the schedule; it does not set a price by itself.
1ddda80b03: The mainnet genesis commits to the hash of a <0>Bitcoin block mined after the launch was announced</0>. That hash is unpredictable, so no Genoryn Krypton block can exist before the announced moment, and everyone, the author included, starts together. Mainnet commits to Bitcoin block <1/> (<2/>), the newest Bitcoin block when the network launched; genesis hash <3/>.

49943c2de1: Genoryn Krypton splits every block's reward among all miners by the work they did, without pools and without luck deciding who takes a whole block.
b05478c1f2: <0>Shares.</0> A header whose proof of work meets <1/> is a share. The network finds about 32 per block; the block itself is one of its miner's shares. Shares are relayed peer to peer and credited by any block within the next 32.
fc784db268: <0>Pool.</0> Each block adds <1/> to a consensus-held pool. Every credited share earns <2/>: the same slice for everyone, so 1 % of the shares earns 1 % of the rewards.
74fc75a2bd: <0>No incentive to censor.</0> A share's credit never depends on which other shares a block includes, so leaving out other miners' shares gains a block finder nothing, and those shares are credited by the next block.
84dc65abaa: <0>Payouts.</0> Credits accrue per miner and are paid as one note every 360 blocks (~6 hours), at most 64 payouts per block, spendable after 100 blocks.
87d4ebdd33: Payout notes are built by consensus from public data (owner, value, height, index) and verified by light wallets against the block header. Specification: <0>docs/spec/rewards.md</0>.
e48b88cc4a: The wallet's Mining tab and <0>genoryn.io/mining</0> carry the same calculator, fed by live data from the chain:
88a04787f4: <0>Join now</0>: from the network's live hashrate, what 1, 10, 100, 1,000 or more GPUs (each like one RTX 5090) would mine: share, GNR a day, month and year, time per GNR, and the value at the market price. The more GPUs join, the smaller each one's share.
f0cb4ed802: <0>The future</0>: choose a year (up to 40 ahead) and how many computers mine; the reward follows the halvings by block height.
61d7cf5467: <0>Scarcity</0>: stock-to-flow by year, next to Bitcoin's and gold's.
df6be0eeb1: <0>Price models</0>, all "what if", none a forecast:
f3a6895137: <0>The work behind one GNR</0>: today's price × how many times more work one GNR takes then (more computers sharing the reward, halvings passed). If 1,000 GNR cost $3 today and 100,000 computers mine later, the same work yields thousands of times fewer GNR.
5ec4b0d8a4: <0>A share of Bitcoin's value</0>: that share of Bitcoin's total value divided by the GNR that exist in the chosen year.
fb9c852e68: <0>People and dollars</0>: a number of people each holding some dollars of GNR, divided by the GNR that exist then.
2316d976e7: Electricity and hardware costs are not counted. The real price is only what people pay each other (<0>Market price</0>).
1845108759: Memory-hard and GPU-first: each hash reads 64 random 128-byte pairs from a dataset, so throughput follows memory bandwidth, the resource that specialised chips gain least on.
fe389ce5b0: <0>Epoch:</0> 16,384 blocks (~11.4 days); seed from the genesis hash and the epoch number.
b29c185f71: <0>Cache:</0> 16 MiB, BLAKE3 chain plus three RandMemoHash passes.
623fcd1afd: <0>Dataset:</0> 2 GiB at launch, +4 MiB per epoch, capped at 12 GiB; each 64-byte item mixes 64 cache items.
91fe5ab00e: <0>Hash:</0> 128-byte mix, 64 dataset accesses with FNV and rotations, final BLAKE3.
512d9ca676: <0>Verification:</0> needs only the cache: about 1 ms per block, so light clients can check proofs of work.
2690d2b7e4: <0>GPU kernels:</0> CUDA and OpenCL, compiled by the GPU driver on first use; a driver whose compiler is broken is reported with a hint to reinstall it.
4971cc10b5: An atomic swap exchanges GNR for bitcoin between two wallets so that either both payments happen or neither does. Both sides lock their coins under the same <0>hash lock</0> (the SHA-256 of a secret) with a <1>timelock</1>: whoever reveals the secret to take one side's coins also lets the other side take theirs, and if nobody does, both refund after their timelocks. No third party ever holds the coins.
2570f7f8fb: <0>Why swaps with bitcoin.</0> Bitcoin's coins are guarded by elliptic-curve signatures, which a large enough quantum computer could break. An atomic swap lets a bitcoin holder move value into GNR, which is guarded by hash-based proofs instead, straight from their own wallet, and swap back the same way at any time. A swap exchanges bitcoin for GNR at the market price; the bitcoin itself stays on Bitcoin's chain with its new owner.
20aea304d9: How a swap runs (GNR locked first)
1e7ca87f88: <0>Agree.</0> A buyer takes a sell offer, or a seller takes a buy offer, on the <1>offer board</1>. The wallets exchange the swap codes through sealed mailboxes, by themselves, within seconds.
4a5b60f646: <0>The seller locks the GNR.</0> The seller's wallet holds the secret and locks exactly the agreed GNR on chain, payable only to the buyer with that secret, or back to the seller after the GNR timelock. Before locking, the seller checks the buyer's terms.
9e8500509b: <0>The buyer checks and pays.</0> The buyer's wallet watches the lock until it has confirmed (see the table) and checks that it is exactly the agreed amount and only the buyer can claim it. Only then does it show where to pay, in a window with the amount, the address and a QR code. The buyer pays within 2 hours into a bitcoin contract with the same hash lock, refundable to the buyer after its own timelock.
2f4025c9c4: <0>The seller takes the bitcoin.</0> Once the payment has confirmed, the seller's wallet claims the bitcoin with the secret, well before the bitcoin timelock. That claim reveals the secret on the Bitcoin chain.
c26388ad07: <0>The buyer takes the GNR.</0> The buyer's wallet reads the secret from the seller's bitcoin claim and claims the GNR with it.
718cd8cd11: A seller who does not have the GNR cannot even list an offer (see <0>proof of funds</0>), and cannot lock what it does not have, so a buyer never pays someone who cannot deliver. The seller cannot take the bitcoin without revealing the secret that releases the GNR to the buyer.
f20c91b2a2: Quick Swap: any amount, in one click
acfb15453b: At the top of the Swap tab (wallet 1.0.46). Say how much you want to buy or sell, in dollars, bitcoin or GNR, and press one button. The wallet finds the best prices among the <0>Quick Swap offers</0> whose makers are online and whose coins are there, and swaps exactly that amount across up to three of them. Each part is its own swap as described above: the seller's GNR is locked first, and either both sides are paid or both keep their coins. See it live on the <1>swap page</1>.
d087e120c4: <0>The price you accepted is the worst you get.</0> A part costs its offer's price. If a part cannot start (someone else took that offer a moment earlier, or its maker stopped answering for two minutes), the wallet replaces it with another offer, never more than 1 % beyond the worst price you were shown.
821e82def0: <0>Never far from the market price</0> (wallet 1.0.48). Quick Swap takes no offer more than 20 % from the market price, or 10 % while the price is still forming or the market is thin. Offers further away stay on the board, marked far from the market, and can still be taken by hand. While the board says the price is catching up with recent swaps, Quick Swap waits.
28552af887: <0>Offers that follow the market.</0> A Quick Swap offer follows the market price by default: it stands at the market price, or a margin above or below it, never past your limit, and comes off the board by itself if the market reaches the trigger price you set.
5a42edd697: <0>Your Bitcoin balance.</0> One address of the wallet's own, from your 24 words. Buying pays from it at once (once it has one confirmation); selling is paid into it; send bitcoin out of it whenever you like, except what running Quick Swaps still need.
fb22facf30: <0>Publishing a Quick Swap offer.</0> Tick Quick Swap when you publish: anyone can swap any part of it, from its smallest part (at least 10,000 sat) up to all of it, at your price. It is listed as up to three lots so several people can swap at once, and after a part the rest of the lot goes back on the board by itself. A Quick Swap buy offer is paid from your Bitcoin balance.
1fe36b3fdf: <0>Bitcoin promised once.</0> Before a seller's wallet locks GNR for a buyer whose bitcoin waits at a deposit, the board adds up what that deposit is already promised to other sellers. A seller locks only if the deposit covers it all, so bitcoin for one swap cannot tie up the GNR of many sellers.
9d69f5bf36: <0>How long.</0> About 10 to 20 minutes for a small part, mostly the bitcoin confirmation. Keep the wallet running and unlocked until it is done.

70943fd017: 3 blocks for a payment up to 0.001 BTC, 6 up to 0.01 BTC, 15 up to 0.1 BTC, 30 above
efe50260d5: Bitcoin confirmations the seller waits for
a4229404bb: 2 hours after the GNR lock has confirmed
d716f0ef0c: 1,260 blocks (about 21 hours); 1,900 (about 32 hours) when the buyer's wallet is older than 1.0.43 from the lock
cb8ba2d8b0: 18 Bitcoin blocks (about 3 hours) from the payment
b71ba8700e: One week; terms that would run longer are refused
71e9c15417: <0>The buyer never pays:</0> the swap ends after the payment window; the seller's GNR returns automatically after its timelock (keep or reopen the wallet then). This is the free option every atomic swap gives the side that pays second: a taker can make a seller's GNR wait out its lock at no cost. It can never take the GNR.
a92b7c79e4: <0>The buyer pays, the seller never claims:</0> the bitcoin returns to the buyer after its timelock. A payment smaller than agreed, or too late to claim safely, is not taken.
cb770ce7be: <0>Either side cancels before anything of theirs is locked:</0> the other side is told through the board and its swap ends too.
94f5baf036: <0>A wallet is closed or locked:</0> the swap waits. Only your wallet holds the keys that lock, claim and refund your coins, so keep it running (the window may be closed) and unlocked until your swaps are done; the timelocks give hours of room.

b3e001ecb9: <0>Proof of work</0>: every offer, message and trade report carries a small proof of work (18 bits, about a second). Longer offers need one more bit for every doubling beyond a day: 21 bits for a week, 23 for a month, 27 for a year, a few seconds on a modern CPU. Keeping junk on the board for long costs as much more as it lasts.
e0ea960d15: <0>Proof of funds</0>: a sell offer is listed only after its GNR is proven. Publishing sets the offer's amount and the fee of its lock aside in a note of its own (merging notes first if the amount is spread over more than two), and the wallet sends the board a zero-knowledge proof that it can spend that note. The proof is an ordinary shielded transfer of the offer's amount to a note fixed by the offer itself, so it fits no other offer, and it is expired from the start, so no block can ever include it: nothing moves. The board checks it, keeps only the nullifiers of the notes behind the offer, takes the offer down the moment one of them is spent, and never lets the same note back two offers, or an offer and a swap in progress. It learns neither your address nor your balance.
784cc86933: <0>While the offer is open</0> the note cannot be sent or put into another offer; the balance card shows it as set aside. A take locks exactly this note.
aa36a382c7: <0>A sell offer commits its GNR for 7 days</0> from the moment it is published. Within that time the GNR can be sold, or go into another sell offer at once and with no new transfer (which starts a new 7 days), but it cannot be sent: not after cancelling, and not after the offer ran its time unsold. Cancelling takes the offer off the board at once. This is a rule of the wallet, kept in its own file. The chain cannot enforce it: it does not see whether a sale was paid in bitcoin, so a seller could always "sell" to themselves; and a wallet restored from its recovery phrase starts without it. What the board and the chain do enforce is that an offer whose GNR moved is no longer listed.
0df68e6a68: <0>Offers for buyers whose bitcoin is ready (from 1.0.43).</0> A sell offer is, by default, only for buyers whose bitcoin is already at an address of their own wallet. Such a buyer's request carries a signature of that address's key; the seller's wallet looks the address up on the Bitcoin chain and locks GNR only if the swap's amount is there, confirmed and unspent. The buyer's wallet then pays the contract by itself. An offer open to every buyer can be published too; for buyers whose bitcoin it has not seen, a wallet holds at most two unpaid locks at a time. The board lists such offers with "pay first".
204ba4b184: <0>One wallet on several computers (from 1.0.43).</0> Every copy of a wallet reports its swaps to a mailbox on the board that only copies of that wallet can find and read: its key derives from the 24 words, the reports are encrypted, and each carries a tag made with the wallet's seed. Another computer with the same wallet shows those swaps with their progress and can carry one on ("Carry on here") if the first computer is switched off or lost. Every step of a swap spends something that can be spent only once, so two computers cannot lock or pay twice; still, keep a swap to one computer.
506385b1a4: <0>When something waits, the wallet says what for.</0> A seller whose buyer did not pay sees the block at which the GNR returns and roughly how many hours that is (the lock cannot be opened sooner by anyone; that is what makes it safe for the buyer). A take that the other wallet does not answer ends by itself after ten minutes. A swap that ran out ends even while the Bitcoin server cannot be reached.
ba7af6de46: <0>Buy offers are paid in advance, to an address of the buyer's own wallet.</0> Bitcoin cannot be put into the swap contract before a seller exists, because the contract names the seller's key and the hash of the seller's secret. So publishing a buy offer shows an address whose key only the buyer's wallet has (it derives from the 24 words). When the bitcoin is there with one confirmation, the wallet posts the offer with a signature of that address's key; the board checks on the Bitcoin chain that the offer's amount is there, unspent, and marks the offer with a ✓ (it keeps the address to itself). When a seller takes the offer and their GNR lock has confirmed, the buyer's wallet pays the contract from the deposit by itself, exactly the agreed amount, and the rest of the swap runs as always. If the offer is cancelled or runs its time, the wallet sends the bitcoin back to the buyer's address; what was set aside for the network fee and not used comes back too. A wallet restored from its 24 words finds such deposits again under Swap, Bitcoin connection, "Bitcoin left from buy offers". A buy offer can still be published without a deposit and paid by hand; it carries no ✓. <1>Buying from a sell offer</1> can be paid in advance the same way: the wallet sends its request to the seller only once the bitcoin is at the deposit address with one confirmation, so the seller's GNR is locked only for a buyer whose bitcoin is ready; if the offer is gone by then, the bitcoin goes back.
ca6f79bba8: <0>The same wallet on two computers.</0> Offers and swaps are kept by the wallet that started them, in its own file; they are not on the chain. A second computer with the same 24 words sees the balance and the GNR locked in a swap ("locked in a swap on another computer", with the block it returns at), but not the swap's progress, and it cannot continue the swap. If the computer that runs the swap is not there when the lock ends, the other one takes the GNR back 30 blocks later. Run the offers and swaps of one wallet on one computer: one copy can spend GNR that the other has set aside.
3db1b0759b: <0>Online and offline</0>: your wallet tells the board every 45 seconds that it is online, for all its offers at once (each proven with its cancel secret). An offer whose maker was seen in the last 2 minutes shows a green dot and can be taken; taking it starts the swap within seconds with no approval. While the maker's wallet is offline the offer stays listed, greyed out, and cannot be taken; after a week offline it is removed and the wallet frees its GNR.
45e6b091c1: <0>Taking</0>: the taker's wallet sends a sealed take message; the maker's wallet answers by itself. An offer is taken once.
bfaf7b8ac0: <0>In progress</0>: a taken offer moves to "in progress" (only its maker can do that, proven against the offer the board stores). It is shown as <1>taken, not paid yet</1> until its maker reports that the bitcoin is in the contract, and only paid swaps count as running: taking an offer costs nothing, and a taker may never pay. The maker's wallet confirms every 10 minutes that the swap still runs and removes the entry as soon as the swap can no longer complete; entries not confirmed for 30 minutes, or older than 12 hours, are dropped.
6266dd9aa8: <0>Limits</0>: up to 5,000 offers, offers of 10,000 sat to 1,000 BTC, mailboxes of 100 messages kept for a day, per-client rate limits.
838df00c32: Offers are anonymous: each has its own one-time X25519 + ML-KEM-1024 key derived from the wallet's swap seed and used for nothing else, never your address.
a90cd1572b: From 1.0.44 an offer can follow the market price instead of standing at a price you chose. Tick <0>Follow the market price</0> when you publish.
3e35c7c04f: <0>What the offer stands for is fixed; what is asked for it moves.</0> A sell offer names its GNR and the bitcoin asked follows the market; a buy offer names its bitcoin and the GNR asked follows the market. Nothing is locked at a price in advance: the price of a sale is the offer's price at the moment the other wallet takes it, and a request with any other amounts is refused.
1e9f83b64e: <0>The wallet moves the price.</0> When the market price is 1 % or more away from the offer's, the wallet takes the offer off the board and lists it again at the new price, with the same GNR (its proof made again) or the same bitcoin deposit behind it. 494d328063: <0>You set a limit, always.</0> A sell offer never asks less than your lowest price; a buy offer never pays more than your highest. b37ecd00ec: <0>Only your wallet can move the price</0>, so it must be running. While it is closed the offer stays at its last price.

24866c8ffc: A 332-byte header commits to the previous block, a Merkle Mountain Range of all earlier blocks, the transactions, the shares, the note-tree root, the nullifiers, the outputs, the payouts and its miner. A block is valid when:
2307a3b6b8: It extends its parent; its timestamp exceeds the median of the last 11 and is at most 300 s in the future.

57332e96b1: The note tree after appending matured payout notes and transfer outputs has the committed root.
938cdf0ee5: Fork choice: the valid chain with the most cumulative work. Side branches are checked for proof of work before storage and fully validated when they become heavier; a branch far behind the main chain is not stored at all. Full specification: <0>docs/spec/consensus.md</0>.
065f8c9c5e: Every transfer spends two notes (one may be a zero-value dummy) and creates two outputs (payment and change). 2cfc3a2b5b: The proof is bound to the exact transaction through its sighash, which replaces a signature. a8d4461bcf: The verifier's wallet (or <0/>, or <1/>) finds the transaction's block and checks it against the chain.

232157af6f: A light wallet trusts nodes for availability only, never for validity:
d665382a8d: <0>Tip.</0> The wallet samples headers (dense near the tip, sparse across history) and checks each one's proof of work and its inclusion in the tip's Merkle Mountain Range; the most recent 91 headers are checked fully, including the difficulty rule. Cost grows with log(chain length).
01231193eb: <0>Checkpoint.</0> Every release carries a checkpoint (mainnet: block 14,800). The chain must contain it; every header above it needs at least 1/16 of its difficulty, and the blocks since it must carry that much work on average.
59cc225177: <0>No future blocks.</0> A header dated more than two hours (plus the 5-minute consensus drift) ahead of your computer's clock is refused, so a fork cannot lower its own difficulty quickly.
12468f97f4: <0>The most work wins.</0> Every MMR node hashes the work beneath it, so the tip proves the total work of the chain. The wallet remembers the most work it has verified and refuses a chain with less. A cheap fork cannot replace the chain it follows, and faking confirmations costs as much work as the honest network spends on them. If a node proves a different block at the wallet's height inside an at least as heavy chain, the wallet goes back to the fork point by itself; a node that only sends bad proofs proves nothing and changes nothing.
c5dac5510f: <0>Blocks.</0> Compact blocks since the wallet birthday are checked against their headers: outputs, nullifiers, payouts and the note-tree root.
63c606c1b9: <0>Witnesses.</0> The wallet downloads a whole 4,096-leaf chunk and computes its own Merkle path, so a node does not learn which note you spend.
79e74d16f7: <0>Cross-checks.</0> Several configured nodes must agree; transactions are sent through all of them.
e3eaa0c731: A wallet that has never synced trusts the first chain shown to it above the checkpoint; for large amounts run your own node or configure several independent ones. Specification: <0>docs/spec/light-client.md</0>.
2d0287758f: Nodes talk to each other over encrypted links. A node is built so that other nodes can never use it against the computer it runs on:
b5b53e0ea7: <0>Encryption:</0> every link starts with an X25519 + ML-KEM-768 handshake and runs ChaCha20-Poly1305 frames.
fa674488b3: <0>Nothing to break into:</0> the networking code is memory-safe Rust with no <1/> code. Peers can only send protocol messages; a node never runs commands, opens files or reaches its own API for them.
294216dbf0: <0>Strict limits:</0> frames of at most 8 MiB (the length is checked before memory is allocated), a cap on every list in a message, 10 seconds for a handshake, at most 64 handshakes at once, 30 seconds for a new peer to introduce itself, at most 4 connections per IP (IPv6: per /64), 64 inbound and 8 outbound peers, a cap on data queued for slow peers.
a40977a0d9: <0>Bans:</0> a peer that sends a malformed message, an invalid block or transaction, or shares without work is disconnected and its IP refused for 24 hours; a flood of useless shares disconnects it.
b45b0c0a29: <0>Address book:</0> peers can only point a node at public internet addresses on unprivileged ports, never at this computer, its local network or special ranges; one network group (IPv4 /16, IPv6 /32) fills at most 16 places, one peer's list is accepted at most once every 10 minutes, and the seeds are always tried first when a node has few peers.
97b07afcd5: <0>Outbound-only by default in the wallet:</0> the full node the wallet starts does not accept incoming connections unless you enable it (Network → <1>Let other nodes connect to my full node</1>), so nothing on the internet can open a connection to your computer.
